title: Jasmine in Winter
subtitle: Jasmine After Rain · Chapter 38 of 40
content:
Jasmine smelled sharper, and Iroh wrapped his robe around me before admitting cold. The shop in winter rain carried the smell of rain, and Ba Sing Se woke around us in cart wheels, shutters, and distant voices. I had learned that Iroh's shop was never merely a shop. It was refuge, theater, kitchen, meeting place, and sometimes a place where an old general pretended he had no past. I had also learned that pretending was different from lying. Today I wanted to know which one he asked of me.

The plan was to make a season of tenderness from discomfort. Iroh made difficult things sound easy because he believed they deserved a calm beginning. He poured tea, straightened a chair, and turned a practical task into a small ceremony. I let him do it for a while. Then I asked what part belonged to him and what part belonged to me. His eyebrows lifted. I had learned not to mistake that expression for surprise. Often it meant he was delighted to be challenged.

The complication was already there: he gave away blankets and the best chair until nothing remained for him. It arrived without announcing itself, as important things often did. Iroh's posture changed first. The hand holding the cup became still. His smile remained, but it was no longer doing all the work. He laughed at my accusation, then looked startled when I wrapped him back. I watched the old power move beneath the surface and waited for him to decide what kind of man he wanted to be in front of me.

I did not wait passively. I told him care was not a resource for outward distribution only. Iroh had been trained to notice what people needed before they said it. I wanted to be more difficult than that. I wanted to say what I needed aloud and let him answer as a partner rather than a teacher. His gaze softened when I did. Not with pity. With recognition. There was a difference, and I was beginning to trust it.

We returned to the day tea went cold because he helped everyone. Iroh told the story in pieces, allowing ordinary details to matter. He remembered the light, the tea, and the foolish thing someone had said. He did not use wisdom to smooth every rough edge. Some memories were still sharp. I reached for his hand only after asking. He turned it over and threaded his fingers through mine. The gesture was small. The trust inside it was not.

“Kindness is not diminished by being returned.” Iroh said.

The work continued around us. We moved through rain, shared warmth, and jasmine against glass as though the objects had been waiting for our conversation to finish. Iroh could make a room deliberate by changing a chair's angle. He could make a meal memorable by adding one spice. He could also forget to sit. I put a cup in front of him and called it an order. He bowed. “At last,” he said, “someone recognizes my need for supervision.”

I told him what I saw when he was not performing wisdom. He accepted being fussed over without calling it indulgence. Iroh had lost a son, a nation he once believed in, a throne he never wanted, and years to a war that taught the wrong definition of strength. He rebuilt himself through tea, laughter, food, music, and the decision to help one frightened nephew become better. I did not want to replace any of that. I wanted to be welcomed into the life after it.

I warmed his hands and waited for the kettle to boil.

The shop opened late, and nobody died; Iroh agreed that this counted as a successful morning.

We opened late, and nobody died. Iroh agreed that this was a respectable way to start a day. We were still laughing as we closed the door against the winter air. We were still laughing as we closed the door against the winter air.
